NIST's GenAI Profile leans on human oversight precisely because inter-rater agreement is the signal that your 'grounded' means the same thing twice — a 94% automated score with no human agreement number behind the gate is a number nobody can defend in an incident review.

A gate with no baseline can only answer 'is this good?' A gate with a baseline answers the question that actually ships product: 'is this better, and did it break anything that already worked?' NIST's AI RMF calls this continuous measurement against a known reference; in practice it is one pinned filename and one pinned baseline run.

WCAG's four principles — Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust (POUR) — are the checklist that turns 'accessibility' from a vibe into an inspectable decision.
This is the WCAG section of the accessibility packet you carry through this module.
Perceivable: color alone carries the meaning, so a colorblind user (or a screen reader) gets nothing (WCAG 1.4.1 Use of Color).
Understandable: red says 'wrong' but never says what to fix (WCAG 3.3.1 Error Identification, 3.3.3 Error Suggestion).
This is WCAG 4.1.2 (Name, Role, Value) satisfied by construction.
WCAG 3.3.1 (Error Identification) — the error is named in code, not just painted.
WCAG 3.3.3 (Error Suggestion) — tell users how to recover, do not just say 'invalid'.
WCAG is the difference you cannot see in a screenshot — which is exactly why it needs an inspection hook, not an eyeball.
The senior tell: automated scanners (axe, Lighthouse) catch roughly a third of WCAG issues — missing alt text, contrast, absent labels — the machine-checkable ones.
WCAG 2.2 AA is the legal bar most regulations point to (ADA, EN 301 549, the European Accessibility Act).

axe covers the machine-checkable slice (~30–40%); the keyboard walkthrough proves Operable (focus order, no traps — WCAG 2.4.3, 2.1.2) and the screen-reader pass proves Understandable + Robust (errors announced with a suggestion — 3.3.1, 3.3.3, 4.1.2).
Prove the WCAG section holds — no vibes, use at least two hooks:
Every interactive element is reachable, focus is always visible, and no keyboard trap exists (WCAG 2.1.2, 2.4.3, 2.4.7).
Each one names WHAT is wrong and HOW to fix it, and moves focus to the problem — not a generic 'submission failed' (WCAG 3.3.1, 3.3.3).
Every field announces its label, role, and current value; errors are announced via role=alert or aria-describedby (WCAG 4.1.2).
On a mobile viewport, Operable shifts to touch-target size (min 44px, WCAG 2.5.8) and Perceivable to reflow at 320px.
